verdict_reasoning: The goal has support in the thread, on the condition that the standard reserves QUALIFY. The list has not chosen between the rewrite patch and the planner-based patch, and each has an open design cost: lost view deparse (standards-compat-2) or duplicated pushdown code (maintenance-fit-1). The claim of standard acceptance also has no source yet (prior-attempts-1). Code review makes sense after these are settled.

brief.title: Add a QUALIFY clause to filter rows on window function results
brief.problem: Users who want to filter on a window function result must wrap the query in a subquery or CTE. The author wants a shorter, more readable form for this common case, which Snowflake, BigQuery, DuckDB and others already offer.
brief.proposed_design: The main patch adds QUALIFY after the WINDOW clause and, after parse analysis, rewrites the query into an inner subquery and an outer query whose WHERE is the QUALIFY condition. The planner then applies existing subquery optimizations such as run conditions and qual pushdown. A second, work-in-progress patch keeps QUALIFY in the planner and covers only conditions that reference window functions.
user_visible_surface: New SELECT clause `QUALIFY condition`, placed after WINDOW and before UNION/ORDER BY/LIMIT.
QUALIFY becomes a fully reserved keyword.
The QUALIFY condition can reference select-list output names; on a name clash the input column wins.
With the rewrite patch, pg_get_viewdef() shows a view defined with QUALIFY in subquery form.
EXPLAIN plans for QUALIFY queries match the equivalent hand-written subquery.
author_claims: The SQL standard committee has accepted the QUALIFY proposal, listed as feature O001.
The rewrite patch gets run conditions and qual pushdown with no new planner code.
The rewrite patch implements the transformation the standard uses to define QUALIFY.
The rewrite patch is complete for window and non-window conditions, with docs and tests.
The author leans toward the planner-based approach for clean view deparse, but it duplicates pushdown logic.
brief.thread_state: Tom Lane and others objected in 2025 to a new reserved word before standardization; Vik Fearing and David Rowley asked for a standard-style rewrite with full pushdown. Since the June 2026 revival only the author has posted, so his question on which design to pursue has no answer yet.
unclear: The material gives no source for standard acceptance, and the doc hunk on conformance is truncated.
The patch does not say which existing applications or extensions use qualify as an identifier and will break.
Neither patch says whether views that use QUALIFY dump and restore with the intended meaning.
The planner-based patch does not say how non-window QUALIFY conditions get filtered, since ExecResult has no per-row qual.
The material does not show whether the crash David Rowley reported with an alias in QUALIFY is fixed in v4.

objections.title: Rewrite design stores views in subquery form, against the reviewer's request
objections.failure_scenario: A user creates a view with QUALIFY, then reads it back with \d+ or pg_dump and gets a nested subquery with generated column names for the projected window functions. If the project later moves to the planner design, the same view deparses differently across major versions. Tools that compare schema dumps then report false differences.
objections.argument: In message #30 Vik Fearing asked that ruleutils print QUALIFY as written, and that any transformation happen in the rewriter. The complete patch rewrites the query during parse analysis instead, and message #38 names the deparse change as its main downside. Choosing the rewrite design fixes the stored form of every QUALIFY view, so a later change of design also changes pg_dump output for views users already have. Neither patch says whether a dumped and restored view keeps its column names and its alias-versus-input-column resolution.
objections.author_must_show: Does a QUALIFY view dumped by pg_dump restore with the same column names and meaning, and which stored form will views keep if the project later switches to the planner design?

critic.reasoning: Message #30 asked that ruleutils print QUALIFY as written, and message #38 names the lost deparse as the main downside of the rewrite patch. Nobody has answered the design question, and neither patch states the dump and restore result.

objections.title: Planner-based design copies window pushdown logic into a second place
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch improves run conditions or qual pushdown below WindowAgg in set_subquery_pathlist() and does not update the QUALIFY path. Hand-written subqueries then get the new plan and QUALIFY queries do not. Nothing fails, so users find out only when they compare EXPLAIN output.
objections.argument: The author leans toward the planner-based patch (message #38) and says it duplicates the run-condition and qual-pushdown code. David Rowley (message #36) said acceptance depends on how much code is reused, and he named a past optimization that would have needed a second copy. Richard Guo (message #37) asked that QUALIFY inherit every existing window optimization. The refactoring of check_and_push_window_quals() into shared helpers is proposed but has not been done.
objections.author_must_show: Can the subquery pushdown helpers be refactored first, as a separate patch, so that QUALIFY and subqueries share a single code path?

critic.reasoning: It applies only to the planner-based patch, which the author prefers. Message #38 confirms the duplication, messages #36 and #37 make reuse a condition, and the shared helpers are not written.

objections.title: Standardization condition from 2025 is claimed but not yet shown
objections.failure_scenario: An application has a table or column named qualify. After an upgrade to a release with this patch, its unquoted queries fail with syntax errors. If the standard later changes the keyword or its scope, the project cannot cite the standard to explain the break.
objections.argument: In messages #4 and #6, Tom Lane accepted the reserved word only once QUALIFY is in the standard, so the breakage can be blamed on SQL:20xx. Vik Fearing agreed in messages #11 and #26 to hold back until then. Message #38 says the proposal is accepted as feature O001 but gives no reference, and the conformance doc hunk is truncated. No reviewer has confirmed the claim since the revival, so the condition from 2025 is still open.
objections.author_must_show: Which standard document or committee decision records QUALIFY as feature O001, with the keyword reserved and the semantics the patch implements?

critic.reasoning: Messages #4, #6 and #11 made standard acceptance the condition for the reserved word. Message #38 states acceptance without a reference, the conformance hunk is truncated, and no reviewer has confirmed it since.

refuted.title: Fully reserved QUALIFY breaks existing identifiers, and the standard status lacks a source
refuted.failure_scenario: An application has a column or function named qualify, used unquoted in a PL/pgSQL function body or in client SQL. After pg_upgrade, pg_dump quotes the name in dumped DDL, but the function body text and the client queries are not rewritten. Those statements fail with a syntax error the first time they run in production.
refuted.argument: Tom Lane's condition in message #6 was that the breakage be justified by "QUALIFY is reserved according to SQL:20xx". Message #38 says the proposal was accepted, and the doc hunk names feature O001, but the material gives no source and the conformance text is truncated. The material does not show whether an optional feature reserves the word in the published standard. The patch also does not say what classes of existing code break, or what release notes would tell users.
refuted.author_must_show: Which published or approved standard text makes QUALIFY a reserved word, and what will the release notes tell users whose code uses qualify unquoted?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1. The thread already accepted the reserved-word breakage once the standard reserves QUALIFY (messages #6, #11), so only the missing source remains open.

refuted.title: Rewrite patch stores QUALIFY views in pg_rewrite in subquery form permanently
refuted.failure_scenario: A user creates a view with QUALIFY on the rewrite patch, and pg_rewrite stores the rewritten two-level query. Every later pg_dump and pg_upgrade carries the subquery text forward, so the user's QUALIFY is never shown again, even if a later release keeps QUALIFY in the Query tree.
refuted.argument: Message #30 asked for the transformation to happen after the stored rule, so that ruleutils can print QUALIFY as written; message #38 accepts the opposite as "the main downside". The thread never settled this. Because the stored form is what pg_upgrade restores, picking the rewrite approach first also fixes the format of existing views. A later switch to the planner approach in message #38 would change only views created after it.
refuted.author_must_show: Is the subquery form in pg_rewrite an accepted permanent representation, or should the Query tree keep a QUALIFY field before any release stores such views?

critic.reasoning: The rewrite patch stores an ordinary subquery Query tree, with no new stored format, and pg_upgrade restores views from pg_dump text. The remaining point, that the QUALIFY spelling is lost, is a duplicate of standards-compat-2.

refuted.title: Parse-analysis rewrite stores the subquery form in every view
refuted.failure_scenario: A user creates a view with QUALIFY on the rewrite patch, and pg_get_viewdef() and pg_dump show a nested subquery instead. If a later release moves QUALIFY into the planner, those views stay in subquery form after dump and upgrade, so the project carries two stored forms of the same clause.
refuted.argument: Vik Fearing (message #30) said parse analysis is the wrong place and that ruleutils should print QUALIFY as written, which would mean rewriting in the rewriter instead. The v4 rewrite patch still rewrites in analyze.c, and message #38 names deparse as its main downside. The stored rule tree is long-lived catalog content, so this choice is hard to undo once views exist in the field.
refuted.author_must_show: Why can the transformation not be done in the rewriter or planner, so that the stored Query keeps a QUALIFY node and ruleutils prints it as written?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. The claim of two stored forms does not hold, because old views would be ordinary subquery views that need no special support.

refuted.title: Non-window QUALIFY needs a new executor filter for one clause
refuted.failure_scenario: To finish the planner-based patch, someone adds a per-row qual loop to ExecResult or a new filter node used only by QUALIFY. Every later executor change, such as JIT or EXPLAIN support, must cover it, and it has no other users to exercise it.
refuted.argument: Message #39 finds that ExecResult cannot filter rows per tuple, and it offers two options: change ExecResult or add a node. The author doubts either would be useful beyond QUALIFY. If ExecResult changes, all queries with a Result node take that path, but the proposal does not say what that costs.
refuted.author_must_show: Which cases besides QUALIFY would use a generic per-row filter node, and what does an ExecResult loop cost queries that do not use QUALIFY?

critic.reasoning: The scenario is about code that neither patch contains, and the complete rewrite patch needs no new executor filter. The cost to queries with a Result node is asserted without support, and message #39 already narrows the cases.

refuted.title: The subquery form already does this, so core inclusion rests on the standard
refuted.failure_scenario: An application that uses qualify as a column or table name breaks on upgrade because the word is now fully reserved. Its users gain nothing they could not already write as a subquery with an outer WHERE. If O001 turns out not to be settled standard text, there is no "the standard requires it" answer to give those users.
refuted.argument: Message #5 states that QUALIFY is semantically equivalent to a subquery plus WHERE, and the rewrite patch claims plans identical to that form, so today the clause is a shorter spelling of an existing idiom. Messages #4, #11 and #26 accepted the reserved word only once the standard requires it. Message #38 asserts acceptance as feature O001, but the material gives no source, and the conformance hunk is truncated. Without that basis, the convenience alone would likely not justify a new fully reserved keyword.
refuted.author_must_show: Which published or committee-approved standard document defines QUALIFY as feature O001 with a reserved keyword and this placement and semantics?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1. The thread weighed the subquery alternative and accepted the clause once standardized (messages #4, #11, #20, #27), so only the missing source remains.

refuted.title: Reserved keyword cost for all, ergonomic gain only for QUALIFY users
refuted.failure_scenario: An application or extension with a column, table or function named qualify upgrades to the release that reserves QUALIFY. Its queries and dumped schemas then fail with a syntax error until every use is double-quoted. The users who gain only save one level of subquery nesting.
refuted.argument: The author and the commit message say QUALIFY is equivalent to a subquery with an outer WHERE (message #5, message #38), so that workaround already works. The demand in the material is mostly that other systems have it (message #1, message #2), plus one user who would like it; no -general or -bugs reports are cited. Tom Lane accepted the breakage only if the standard reserves the word (message #4, message #6). The material claims acceptance as feature O001 but gives no source, and the conformance doc hunk is truncated.
refuted.author_must_show: Where is the accepted standard text that reserves QUALIFY as feature O001, and is there Postgres user demand beyond porting from other systems?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1. The thread weighed the reserved-word cost against the gain and accepted it on standardization (messages #6, #11), and messages #1, #2 and #9 show demand from other systems and the committee.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: Both patches change parsenodes.h, and the planner-based patch also changes optimizer/paths.h.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a QUALIFY clause and makes QUALIFY a fully reserved keyword.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: The planner-based patch adds QUALIFY pushdown and run conditions in allpaths.c and planner.c.

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: With the rewrite patch, a view defined with QUALIFY deparses and dumps in subquery form.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The new reserved word breaks unquoted uses of qualify as an identifier on upgrade.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The planner-based patch keeps a second copy of the window pushdown logic that later patches must update.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which standard document or committee decision records QUALIFY as feature O001, with the keyword reserved and the semantics the patch implements?
Does a view defined with QUALIFY dump and restore with the same column names and the same alias-versus-input-column resolution under the rewrite patch?
Can the subquery pushdown helpers be refactored first, as a separate patch, so that QUALIFY and subqueries share one code path?
How does the planner-based patch filter QUALIFY conditions that contain no window function?
Is the crash David Rowley reported with an alias in QUALIFY fixed in v4, and does a regression test cover it?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the grammar and keyword policy, and one who knows window function planning. Committers commented earlier in the thread, but none has posted since the June 2026 revival.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a permanent reserved keyword, the stored and dumped form of QUALIFY views, and, with the planner-based patch, a second pushdown path to keep in step.
committability.author_follow_up: The author revived the thread in June 2026, posted v4 with two alternative patches, and kept the entry rebased across three CommitFests.

priority.reason: Several other systems ship QUALIFY and users migrating from them gain, but the choice between two patches of about 86 KiB each is open. Reviewing either in detail before that choice risks wasted work.

provisional_note: Without the code, it cannot be checked that the rewrite keeps column-privilege checks for columns used only in QUALIFY, or that the rewritten query gives the same results in all cases with DISTINCT, aggregates and set operations.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Implement <null treatment> for window functions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the SQL-standard RESPECT NULLS and IGNORE NULLS syntax to all true window functions, without hardcoding the standard's list of functions, and adds TREAT NULLS to CREATE FUNCTION. It does not implement FROM LAST.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch failed to compile under GCC with -Werror because 'step' may be used uninitialized in WinGetFuncArgInPartition and WinGetFuncArgInFrame. No new version came in for two months, so Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This was two months ago, so this patch has been marked as returned
with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: window function improvements WIP
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch first allowed DISTINCT inside aggregates used as window functions, such as array_agg(DISTINCT week) over a frame, with code limited to int, float and numeric. After review the author stopped that work and posted a different patch that adds RESPECT/IGNORE NULLS to lag(), lead(), first_value(), last_value() and nth_value(), with negative positions in nth_value() to read the frame in reverse.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane asked whether DISTINCT on a window function is well defined, given one output row per input row and order sensitivity. He also objected to datatype-specific code, so the author suspended the DISTINCT work. Surafel Temesgen's review of the null treatment patch found white space errors, uncommented functions, oversized regression tests and an unexplained change to makeBoolAConst. The author then judged Vik Fearing's competing <null treatment> patch the better design and offered to withdraw his own, and Michael Paquier closed the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think that Vik Fearing's patch about "Implement <null treatment> for window functions" is much clear, better and has a chance to be committed.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add SQL syntax check
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a --syntax option to the postgres server binary that reads SQL from standard input, runs it through the raw parser only (no catalog access or parse analysis), and reports whether it is valid SQL via a message and exit code. The intent was to support manual and automated script checks and editor integrations.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Several reviewers held that the feature did not belong in the postgres binary, and Robert Haas marked the entry Rejected on that basis. The main objection, attributed to Tom Lane and endorsed by Robert Haas, was that the check exposes an implementation detail, the division of work between gram.y (raw_parser) and parse analysis, so it would miss things users consider syntax errors and flag things that seem semantic. Making that work would need a much larger effort and a different design. Robert Haas also noted that the 45-line patch had no comments, tests or documentation, and the author agreed to the rejection.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I strongly suspect that doing something useful in this area requires
about two orders of magnitude more code than are included in this
patch, and a completely different design.

precedents_retrieved.title: possibility to write window function in PL languages (like PLpgSQL)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets users write window functions in PL/pgSQL, using a special windowobject variable and SQL-callable wrappers around the C WindowObject API. Values fetched from the window arguments come back through a new proxy type, typedvalue, which PL/pgSQL assignment casts to the target variable's type.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane rejected the typedvalue type: its hard-wired set of conversions would have to grow to cover every built-in cast and could not handle extension types. He proposed dedicated PL/pgSQL syntax instead, and said access to partition local memory should stay out of a first version. The author withdrew the entry, saying a direct mapping of the WindowObject API looks like Cobol and that the declarative syntax needs a different concept.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: That seems like a conceptual mess, a performance loss, and a permanent maintenance time sink.

precedents_retrieved.title: Consider parallel for LATERAL subqueries having LIMIT/OFFSET
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes set_rel_consider_parallel so that a lateral subquery with LIMIT/OFFSET may still be considered for parallel query, so a Gather can go above the whole nested loop. A later version allows this only when rel->lateral_relids is not empty.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author argued that each outer row gets its own execution of the limited subquery, but Tom Lane (seen only in quoted text) and Robert Haas were not convinced this is safe. Tom Lane noted that the patch took any lateral dependency as enough, even one that does not feed the limited subquery. Robert Haas said the real issue is where parameters are set and used, which the LATERAL keyword does not capture. The commitfest manager returned it because no further review was coming, and asked for a more rigorous correctness argument or simpler constraints.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The problem here isn't created by LATERAL, but by parameters.

precedents_retrieved.title: [PATCH] Add UPDATE WHERE OFFSET IN clause
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds `UPDATE ... WHERE OFFSET n IN cursor`, which updates a row from the last FETCH by a zero or negative index, so ECPG cursor readahead can update rows without a MOVE before `WHERE CURRENT OF`. It works only for `SELECT FOR UPDATE` cursors and records the rows read in nodeLockRows.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that OFFSET n means "the row read N reads ago", which breaks with non-linear FETCH/MOVE and exposes implementation details such as reading backwards or rewinding. He also objected that nodeLockRows would use unbounded memory for every query, cursor or not. The author answered that he was only testing the idea, and no revised patch followed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It looks
to me like "OFFSET n" really means "the row that we read N reads ago",
not "the row N before the current cursor position".

precedents_retrieved.title: Use JOIN USING aliases in ruleutils.c
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes ruleutils.c so that, when JOIN USING output columns conflict with other names in a query, it attaches generated JOIN USING aliases (a feature added in Postgres 14) and qualifies the columns with them. This replaces the old approach of renaming those columns to be unique across the whole query.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the new output would reduce pg_dump portability, since dumped views would no longer load into pre-v14 servers or other database systems. He also saw little gain: the patch added code to ruleutils.c on net, and the regression test output was not clearly better. The author agreed and withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
My big fear is that it will reduce portability of pg_dump output:
views that would have loaded successfully into pre-v14 servers
no longer will, and your chances of porting them to other RDBMSes
probably go down too.

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallelize correlated subqueries that execute within each worker
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner build parallel plans for queries with correlated subplans when each subplan runs entirely within one parallel worker, so no Param value has to pass between workers. After review, the design changed to treat PARAM_EXEC params as parallel safe by default, track required params on each rel, and insert a Gather node only where that set is empty.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread shows no author reply after Tomas Vondra's July 2024 review, and the entry was returned with feedback in October 2024. That review found that regression tests failed on a changed plan in select_parallel, reported a compiler warning, and listed code comments. It also said no reviewer was able to confirm that the PARAM handling is correct.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: And in general the patch looks reasonably simple and clean, but my knowledge of PARAM intricacies is pretty much nil, so I'm hesitant to claim the patch is correct.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent covers QUALIFY. [P7] is about ruleutils output for JOIN USING aliases, and its portability reason does not apply here. The only earlier objection is in this thread: the conditional acceptance in messages #4 and #6.
Two objections raised. Placement after WINDOW and name resolution with input columns winning match what reviewers asked for in messages #10 and #15, so those points are not raised.

Neither patch touches WAL, relation files, SLRUs, the control file or the wire protocol. The only persistent state is the stored rule for views, covered above. [P7] concerns dump portability to older servers and does not apply here.

QUALIFY adds no new privilege, object type or exposure path. It filters rows the user can already read in a query the user writes. RLS, column privileges and security_barrier quals still apply to the base relations in both designs, and pushdown into security barrier views uses the existing leakproof checks. Without the code, it cannot be checked that the rewrite keeps column-privilege checks for columns used only in QUALIFY.
Reserved-keyword breakage and the claim of standard acceptance are left to other angles. No committer has posted since the June 2026 revival, so nobody has answered the design question.
Only one objection from this angle. No extension can add SELECT grammar, so if the standard status is confirmed, the existing subquery idiom does not by itself argue against core placement.

Demand is partly shown: many other systems ship QUALIFY, and migrations from them would benefit. The only demand-side objection is that the reserved-word cost depends on a standard status the material does not verify.
